condition.notes: Rail voltage is present and nominally in tolerance but unstable (oscillating / drooping). The DC reading is fine but the AC content is excessive. Common causes: output capacitor ESR high (dried electrolytic), feedback compensation network degraded, or load transients the loop cannot track.

next_steps.action: Rail voltage is UNSTABLE (in tolerance on the DMM but oscillating on the scope). Measure the output ripple with an oscilloscope (AC-coupled, 20 MHz bandwidth limit) and check the output capacitor ESR.

measure.what: Output ripple (peak-to-peak mV) and output capacitor ESR
measure.where: Output capacitor + terminal to ground (scope); output cap legs (ESR meter or DMM)
measure.instrument: Oscilloscope AC-coupled 20MHz BW + ESR meter (or DMM resistance as a rough proxy)
measure.expected: Ripple typically <30 mVpp for a buck, <50 mVpp for an LDO. Output cap ESR typically <0.1 ohm for a good polymer/tantalum, <0.5 ohm for aluminium. Values much higher indicate a dried cap.
measure.safety: Powered measurement. Use a 10x probe; ground the probe tip to the ground plane near the cap, not at a remote point.

interpretations.then: Output capacitor is degraded (dried electrolytic). Replace with a cap of the same value, voltage rating, AND low ESR (polymer or low-ESR aluminium). Verify ripple drops after replacement.

Loop is unstable — likely a feedback compensation cap dried or the wrong compensation. Check the controller's compensation network (Type II/Type III components). This requires the controller datasheet.
interpretations.requires_info_note: Compensation network values are controller-specific; consult the controller datasheet.

interpretations.then: The 'unstable' reading may have been a measurement artifact (probe ground loop, aliasing). Re-measure with a short ground spring. If still unstable, the issue may be load transients — capture a single-shot trigger on the transient.
